sections.h: 3 John: Gaius, the brothers and Diotrephes
sections.b: 3 John is the New Testament's fullest picture of Christian hospitality at work. Gaius received traveling brothers, "strangers at that" (3 John 1:5), who "take nothing from the Gentiles" (3 John 1:7), and the Elder asks him to "send them on their journey in a way worthy of God" (3 John 1:6): to supply them for the road. Supporting them makes the host one of the "fellow workers for the truth" (3 John 1:8). Diotrephes is the opposite: he will not receive them and drives out those who do (3 John 1:10).

common: 3 John treats support for traveling missionaries as a share in their work.

sections.b: 3 John mentions at least two churches and implies a third: the church where the brothers reported Gaius' love (3 John 1:6), the church where Diotrephes "loves to be first" (3 John 1:9), and Gaius' own circle of "friends" (3 John 1:14). Travelers and letters linked them, and a local leader could refuse both, and even expel members (3 John 1:10).

The writer of 2 and 3 John calls himself simply "the Elder," a title of standing that he expects everyone to recognize (3 John 1:1). His authority is personal: he writes letters, sends envoys, and plans to come and deal with Diotrephes before the church (3 John 1:10). Diotrephes, "who loves to be first," holds enough power in his own church to refuse the Elder and expel members. Adolf von Harnack saw in him the earliest single local bishop whose name survives. Plummer thought he wanted to make his church independent of the Elder, and that whether he was its elder "cannot be either affirmed or denied."

sections.h: 3 John: expulsion used against the Elder's people
sections.b: Diotrephes "drives out of the church" those who want to receive the traveling brothers (3 John 1:10), the same verb used when the man born blind was driven out of the synagogue (John 9:34). Here exclusion is the wrong done, not the remedy: the Elder promises to bring Diotrephes' works before the church. Set beside 2 John 1:10, which forbids receiving false teachers, the letter shows how the power to shut the door could serve the truth or be turned against it.

The KJV's "I wish above all things that thou mayest prosper and be in health" (3 John 1:2, KJV) became a key text for the prosperity teaching: Oral Roberts said his Bible fell open at this verse in 1947. The Greek says "in every way," not "above all things"; the verb means to get on well, not to grow rich; and the wish for health was the ordinary opening of a Greek letter (Papyrus Oxyrhynchus 292, about AD 25). It is a friend's prayer for a friend.

uncommon: 3 John 2 shows God's will to make believers wealthy and healthy (the prosperity teaching of Oral Roberts and others).

sections.b: The Elder prays that Gaius is "in good health" (3 John 1:2), using the everyday wish of Greek letters. Plummer saw in it "good authority for praying for temporal blessings for our friends." Oral Roberts, who said this verse began his healing ministry, read it as God's will for believers; Plummer read it as a prayer for a friend, "a model for all friendly wishes of good fortune to others."

Jewish speech uses "the Name" for God's own name (Leviticus 24:11). The early Christians used the same phrase for the name of Jesus: the apostles were "dishonored for the sake of the Name" (Acts 5:41), and the traveling brothers of 3 John set out "for the sake of the Name" (3 John 1:7). 3 John never says "Jesus" or "Christ" at all.

3 John shares less with 1 John than 2 John does, but its rule "Anyone who does good is from God. Anyone who does bad has not seen God" (3 John 1:11) is 1 John in brief (1 John 3:6, 10; 1 John 4:20), and its love of "truth" and "testimony" runs through all three letters.
